title: Preseason practice: a confused lineman after sprints
objective: Recognize exertional heat stroke (core temperature usually above 40 C with CNS dysfunction such as confusion, ataxia or seizures), cool by ice-water immersion, and track rectal temperature, stopping at 38 to 39 C
secondaryObjectives: Emergency management and athlete safety: spine-injury management, sudden cardiac arrest, heat illness and the emergency action plan

brief.situation: 15:30 at a high school's preseason football practice, the second practice of a hot, humid day. You are the sports physical therapist covering practice. Jordan, 17, a lineman, stumbles off the field after conditioning sprints, then sits down hard on the bench, glassy-eyed.
handover: The emergency action plan names you to lead on the field. A cold-water immersion tub is filled with ice water beside the bench; ice towels, a rectal thermometer and the AED are in your kit.
The coaches and two student aides can help. Phone coverage is good; EMS takes about 10 minutes to reach the field.
His parent is in the stands.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time at the pace you choose: study pace (3x) or exam realism (1x). Pause any time.
Each check takes the time on its button. His core temperature responds to what you do.
Partway through you are asked to write your reasoning. A debrief scores what you did.

source.note: With exercise stopped but no cooling in the heat, his core temperature creeps up. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.

parts.label: Recognition
parts.criteria: Collapse in the heat with confusion, slurred speech and ataxia (CNS dysfunction) and a rectal temperature above 40 C: exertional heat stroke, not heat exhaustion; oral or skin temperatures cannot rule it out.
parts.modelAnswer: This is exertional heat stroke until proven otherwise: he collapsed after sprints in the heat, he is confused, slurring and ataxic, and his rectal temperature is over 40 C. An oral reading would mislead me.

parts.label: Action
parts.criteria: Ice-water immersion at once on site; 911 with the plan to cool first and transport second; rectal temperature tracked; out of the tub at about 38.9-39 C; within 30 minutes of collapse; hand over to EMS after cooling.
parts.modelAnswer: Into the ice-water tub now, call 911 and say we will cool first, then transport. Track rectal temperature, take him out at about 39 C, aiming to get there within 30 minutes of collapse, then hand him to EMS with the timeline.

expertPath.text: Mental status: confused, slurred, ataxic. Rectal temperature: about 41.4 C (106.5 F). Exertional heat stroke.
Into the ice-water tub, an aide holding him. Call 911: heat stroke, cooling on site, cool first then transport.
Rectal temperature reaches 39 C: out of the tub, on his side. Tell his parent.
Hand him to EMS with the timeline and his temperatures.

organInjury.headline: Still hot at 30 minutes
organInjury.body: Every minute above 40 C adds injury. Immersion in ice water is the fastest way down; towels, fans and ice packs are far slower.

hotTransport.headline: Transported before cooling
hotTransport.body: Cool first, transport second: an ambulance or car ride wastes the minutes that matter. Cool on site to about 39 C, then transport.

cooledFirst.headline: Cooled first, then transported
cooledFirst.body: You confirmed heat stroke with a rectal temperature and CNS signs, immersed him at once, stopped at about 39 C and then handed over to EMS. That is the expert path.

cooledGaps.headline: Cooled, with gaps
cooledGaps.body: Check how fast immersion started, whether a rectal temperature guided it, and where you stopped (about 38.9-39 C, not lower).

time_up.headline: Still on the field
time_up.body: Heat stroke is treated on site. Recognize, immerse, measure, then transport.

scoring.modelReasoning: Collapse after sprints in the heat with confusion, slurred speech and ataxia is exertional heat stroke until a rectal temperature says otherwise; oral and skin readings are unreliable in an exercising athlete. The statement's diagnosis is CNS dysfunction with a core temperature above 105 F (40.5 C). Cold-water immersion is the most effective treatment and should start on site at once, aiming below 102.5 F (39.2 C) within 30 minutes of collapse; stop at about 38.9-39 C to avoid overcooling. Call 911 but cool first and transport second, then hand over with the timeline.
